bigPicture: The Middle East war spread risk to a second sea gateway: Yemen's government-aligned forces pulled back from the Bab al-Mandeb strait to defend Aden, while the Houthis kept firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia and Bahrain condemned Iran's attacks on an air base used by US forces. In the US, President Trump blamed the previous administration for the air-traffic meltdown that cancelled more than 15,000 flights and asked Congress for money, and Treasury Secretary Bessent told Nvidia's board to hire an outsider as CEO. Stock markets were closed for the weekend, so market figures are Friday's closing levels; oil futures reopen on Sunday evening.

glossary.def: A narrow passage, such as a strait, that a large share of ships or trade must pass through, so trouble there affects many countries.
glossary.example: Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden on the route to the Suez Canal.

glossary.def: The article of the UN Charter that recognises a state's right to self-defence if an armed attack occurs, until the Security Council acts.
glossary.example: Iran cited Article 51 to call its strikes on US bases in Bahrain defensive; Bahrain called them aggression.

glossary.def: Government rules that limit the sale of certain goods or technologies, such as advanced chips, to particular countries or buyers.
glossary.example: Bessent asked Nvidia's board to answer questions about its compliance with export restrictions.

glossary.def: An illegal payment returned to an official in exchange for steering a contract, usually by inflating the price the public pays.
glossary.example: Hungarian prosecutors suspect a former minister of taking kickbacks on overpriced second-hand buses.

glossary.def: A second round of voting between the top candidates when no one wins an outright majority in the first round.
glossary.example: Cape Verde will hold a run-off on 29 November if no presidential candidate passes 50%.

glossary.def: Money that people working abroad send home to family, often a large part of income in small or poor economies.
glossary.example: More Cape Verdeans live abroad than at home, so their transfers matter to the islands' economy.

glossary.def: A legal requirement for citizens, usually young men, to serve in the armed forces for a set period.
glossary.example: Germany's 'Gen Z' protesters oppose plans to revive compulsory military service.

glossary.def: The formal handing over of a suspect by one country to another that wants to prosecute them.
glossary.example: Burkina Faso issued 14 warrants with extradition requests for exiled journalists and critics.

glossary.def: Finding and monitoring people who were near an infected person so they can be isolated quickly if they fall ill.
glossary.example: Violence in eastern Congo stops Ebola teams from tracing contacts.

glossary.def: The main political statement at a UN climate summit, agreed by consensus, that sums up the overall outcome.
glossary.example: A first draft of COP31's cover decision is expected early in the final week.

glossary.def: Cash plus bank deposits and similar short-term bank liabilities held by households and firms.
glossary.example: Poland's M3 was 2,973.1 bn zł in September 2026, of which cash was about 16.8%.

glossary.def: Money that banks hold in accounts at the central bank and use to settle payments with each other.
glossary.example: When a customer pays someone at another bank, reserves move between the two banks.

glossary.def: A bank's highest-quality capital (mainly shareholders' equity) divided by its risk-weighted assets; Basel rules set a 4.5% minimum plus buffers.
glossary.example: A bank with 4.2 bn zł of CET1 and 50 bn zł of risk-weighted assets has a ratio of 8.4%.

glossary.def: What a bank earns on loans and securities minus what it pays on deposits and funding, divided by its interest-earning assets.
glossary.example: Earning 7% on loans and paying 2.5% on deposits gives a margin of several percentage points.

glossary.def: A fund that repays depositors up to a limit if a bank fails, which reduces the risk of bank runs.
glossary.example: Poland's BFG covers up to €100,000 per depositor per bank, repaid within 7 working days.

stocks.overview: With most exchanges closed, the main company news came from Washington: Treasury Secretary Bessent said Nvidia should hire an outside CEO and answer export-control questions within 10 days, adding pressure before its results on Tuesday 17 November. President Trump blamed the previous administration for the air-traffic meltdown that has touched airlines and contractor L3Harris, as cancellations passed 15,000 over Friday and Saturday. In Riyadh, Aramco rose about 1% in Sunday trading while the broader Saudi index slipped. All other prices are Friday's closes.

stories.everyday: Goods from Asia to Europe, including to Poland, often travel through the Red Sea; longer routes add days and cost, which can eventually show up in the prices of imported goods and fuel.
stories.rankWhy: Bab al-Mandeb is the southern gate of the Red Sea, on the main Asia–Europe shipping route to the Suez Canal; a Houthi foothold there adds a second chokepoint risk while Hormuz is already disrupted.
stories.title: Yemen's government-aligned forces pull back from the Bab al-Mandeb strait to defend Aden, as the Houthis keep firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia
stories.what: On Sunday the Southern Armed Forces, a group allied with Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, said they were redeploying from Dhubab airport and the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to prioritise defending Aden, the government's interim capital, and nearby provinces. Xinhua reported the move follows Houthi seizures of strategic positions in Lahj province, which set back a coalition-backed offensive; Al Jazeera said the Houthis say they are preparing to advance on Aden. A government forces spokesman asked the international community to help restore control over Bab al-Mandeb and Yemen's west coast. Earlier on Sunday the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh and several drones aimed at regions including Mecca and the Eastern Province (Al Jazeera counted five drones, Gulf News six; sources differ); Saudi authorities say at least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia since 23 September.
stories.why: A chokepoint is a narrow sea passage that a large share of trade must use. Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, so ships between Asia and Europe pass it on the way to the Suez Canal (Xinhua). If the armed group that attacked shipping there in past years controls more of the coast, shipowners and insurers may treat the route as riskier, which can mean longer voyages around Africa and higher freight costs, at a time when the Strait of Hormuz is already dangerous.

stories.everyday: More danger in the Gulf keeps oil and gas prices high and volatile, which feeds through to fuel and heating bills in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Iran is now openly targeting a Gulf state that hosts US forces, which raises the risk of a wider regional war around the world's main oil-exporting area.
stories.title: Bahrain accuses Iran of 'aggression' after Sunday's attacks on an air base used by the US; Iran says neighbours helped the US attack it
stories.what: Bahrain's Foreign Ministry denounced a 'resumption of Iran's aggression' after early-Sunday attacks on Riffa Air Base, which the US military uses, and said it holds Iran fully responsible; its military said air defences intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks. Iran's Revolutionary Guards had said they sent six drones at a US radar at the base. At a news conference on Sunday, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said regional countries had helped the US attack Iran, cited the self-defence article of the UN Charter (Article 51) and called Iran's strikes purely defensive. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that Iran would widen the geographical scope of the conflict if the US 'makes a mistake'. Jordan and Egypt condemned the attacks on Bahrain.
stories.why: Bahrain hosts US military facilities, so Iran presents strikes there as hitting US assets, while Gulf governments see an attack on their own territory. Each new front raises the chance that oil installations or shipping are hit, which is why traders watch such statements before oil futures reopen. Al Jazeera's correspondent noted Iran had held back for weeks but has now fired at Bahrain twice in three days.

stories.everyday: Travellers face cancelled flights and lost days; under US rules, passengers get a refund if a flight is cancelled and they choose not to travel, but hotels and meals are usually not covered when the cause is outside the airline's control.
stories.rankWhy: The worst US aviation disruption since 2001 hit millions of travellers, and the political fight over who pays for modernising air traffic control has begun.
stories.title: Trump breaks his silence on the US air-traffic meltdown, blames the Biden administration and asks Congress for money; cancellations top 15,000
stories.what: On Sunday President Donald Trump posted that the upgrade of the air-traffic control system should not happen in 'drips and drabs' and that Congress should approve more money, and he blamed the Biden administration for the system's state (AP via PBS). FlightAware counted 9,138 US cancellations on Friday and 6,693 on Saturday, and more than 1,400 by Sunday morning (Yahoo News). Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began when contractor L3Harris was replacing copper lines with fibre and a router flooded the system; officials are still checking whether the router was misconfigured or defective. The FAA said schedules should return to normal by the end of Sunday.
stories.why: Air traffic control is a network: when one router floods it with data, facilities far away can lose communications, so the safest response is to stop departures. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA last year, which Duffy calls a down payment (AP). The outage strengthens calls for more spending but also raises questions about how upgrades are managed.

stories.everyday: Nvidia shares are large weights in US indices and many pension and index funds, so turmoil there can affect savings worldwide.
stories.rankWhy: Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies and its chips drive the AI boom, so pressure from the US Treasury over its leadership and export compliance matters for the whole tech sector.
stories.title: US Treasury Secretary Bessent says Nvidia must 'go outside the company' for a new CEO and answer export-control questions within 10 days
stories.what: Speaking on Fox News' 'Sunday Morning Futures', Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for Jensen Huang's successor and called for a 'dramatic shakeup' (Reuters via KFGO). He said the board and its outside lawyers must answer questions about the company's compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, one of them reportedly involving a suspected Chinese spy. The Financial Times reported on Friday that the board had approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas.
stories.why: Export controls are rules that limit which advanced chips can be sold to China; if regulators believe a company broke them, it can face fines or tighter limits on sales. A senior official publicly pressing a private company's board is unusual and adds uncertainty for investors already selling chip stocks after Huang's exit.

stories.everyday: Residents and truck drivers in Russia have about two weeks to return; cross-border family visits and some freight will have to take long detours.
stories.rankWhy: A NATO and EU member shutting its road border with Russia over sabotage shows how hybrid attacks are hardening Europe's eastern frontier.
stories.title: Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia from 1 December after an attempted arson attack on a drone maker it blames on Russia's GRU
stories.what: Estonia's government said on Sunday it will close its three open road crossings with Russia (Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula) on 1 December; Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna did not say how long the closure will last (ERR, Al Jazeera). On Saturday morning eight Latvian citizens were detained after allegedly trying to break into and set fire to the premises of Threod Systems, which makes reconnaissance and attack drones, near Tallinn. Estonia's Internal Security Service attributed the plot to Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU; it is the second attempted arson at an Estonian defence company since August. Moscow had not commented immediately.
stories.why: Officials argue that fewer crossings mean fewer chances for people recruited by Russian services to move in and out. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia must be prepared to reduce the risks it faces.

stories.everyday: Attacks on power grids mean blackouts and cold homes for Ukrainians; damage to Russian refineries can tighten fuel supply in Russia and add to volatility in diesel markets.
stories.rankWhy: Strikes deep inside Russia on refining and petrochemical plants affect Russia's fuel output and show the war's reach as peace talks continue.
stories.title: Ukraine says it hit a major petrochemical complex and a refinery in Tatarstan, more than 1,000 km from its border, and a helicopter-parts plant in Bryansk
stories.what: Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Nizhnekamskneftekhim synthetic rubber complex and the TAIF-NK refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Tatarstan, overnight into Sunday, hitting the refinery's main crude distillation unit and starting fires (Kyiv Post). It also reported a strike on the Monolit aircraft and helicopter components plant in Trubchevsk, Bryansk region. Nizhnekamsk's mayor acknowledged drone damage in the city's industrial zone. Kyiv Independent reported that Russia launched 132 long-range drones overnight, 106 of which Ukraine said it intercepted, and that a Russian attack on the Odesa region temporarily cut power to about 41,000 families.
stories.why: Ukraine targets refineries to reduce Russia's fuel production and export income, which helps finance the war; Russia targets Ukraine's power grid to weaken its economy and morale before winter. Both sides keep striking while US-led talks continue.

stories.everyday: If more Russian drones reach substations, more Ukrainian households face blackouts in winter.
stories.rankWhy: A speed cap on satellite terminals affects Ukraine's ability to protect its power grid from Russian drones as winter begins.
stories.title: Zelensky says a speed limit on SpaceX's Starshield terminals stops Ukrainian interceptor drones from downing Russian jet-powered drones
stories.what: President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday that restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet, cap terminals at about 161 km/h (100 mph) along the front line and over occupied territory, which prevents Ukrainian interceptor drones from catching Russia's jet-powered Shahed drones (Kyiv Independent). He linked this to successful Russian strikes on electricity substations and told his ministries to work with US officials and SpaceX to lift the limits before winter. A bipartisan US Congressional Ukraine Caucus demanded a full explanation and restored access. The report did not include a response from SpaceX or the US government.
stories.why: Interceptor drones need fast, reliable data links to chase targets; if the link stops working above a certain speed, fast enemy drones can escape. The case shows how much modern militaries depend on privately owned technology and the decisions of the companies and governments that control it.

stories.everyday: Much of the world's trade, including goods heading to Europe, passes through the South China Sea; stability there helps keep supply chains and prices steady.
stories.rankWhy: ASEAN's positions on the South China Sea, Myanmar and migrant workers shape a fast-growing region.
stories.title: ASEAN summit opens in Manila: Timor-Leste joins as the 11th member, but a South China Sea code of conduct with China is not finalised
stories.what: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr opened the 49th ASEAN Summit on Sunday, urging unity amid geopolitical tension, economic uncertainty and climate change (AP via ABC News; Daily Tribune). A new emblem marked Timor-Leste's admission as the bloc's 11th member, and Cyprus, Slovakia and Slovenia joined ASEAN's Treaty of Amity and Cooperation. The Daily Tribune reported that negotiations on a South China Sea code of conduct are about 80% complete but were not finalised, and that Myanmar remains excluded from high-level meetings. Draft statements seen by AP call for restraint in the South China Sea and Myanmar and for measures to shield economies from the Middle East war.
stories.why: A code of conduct would set rules for behaviour in waters claimed by China and several ASEAN members; without it, clashes at sea remain a risk to one of the world's busiest trade routes. ASEAN decides by consensus, so members aligned with the US or China often settle on cautious wording.

stories.everyday: This is a humanitarian story: it shows how housing, water and health are linked, and why aid access matters most in winter.
stories.rankWhy: About a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas as winter begins, with infections already rising.
stories.title: WHO warns 'the worst is yet to come' in Gaza as respiratory infections rise and winter floods hit tents
stories.what: Acute respiratory infections in Gaza are 33,000 cases higher than a year earlier and make up 11% of consultations, the WHO's representative in the occupied Palestinian territory, Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, told reporters (Reuters, published 15 Nov). The WHO says nearly 1 million displaced people live in flood-exposed areas, 400,000 of them in extremely high-risk zones, after heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents. COGAT, the Israeli body that coordinates aid, said it has allowed in all requested medicines and that more than 93,000 tents have entered since its winter plan began. The WHO says it struggles to bring in laboratory supplies.
stories.why: Damp, crowded shelters encourage mould and bacteria and let infections spread, especially among young children; floodwater can contaminate drinking water. Reuters reported that overcrowding has worsened as the Israeli military moves the 'Yellow Line' set under the October ceasefire; the military rejects claims it deliberately shrinks the civilian area.

stories.everyday: Insecurity and disease together keep millions of Congolese displaced and poor; outbreaks there are also watched closely by health authorities worldwide.
stories.rankWhy: Massacres in Ebola-hit eastern Congo kill civilians and slow the response to the country's largest-ever Ebola outbreak.
stories.title: At least 44 civilians killed in Islamic State-linked ADF raids in Congo's Ituri province, an Ebola hotspot
stories.what: Fighters of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), an Islamic State-linked group formed by former Ugandan rebels, killed at least 44 civilians in villages of Mambasa territory in Ituri province, humanitarian and security sources told AFP (Africanews, 14 Nov). A local official said victims were hacked with machetes or shot. Days earlier, an attack in neighbouring North Kivu killed 66 people, including three health workers. The WHO's latest outbreak report counts 10,668 confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola cases and 5,198 deaths in Congo as of 3 November, the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded there.
stories.why: WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has called the region's instability one of the greatest obstacles to the Ebola response: violence stops health workers from tracing contacts and isolating patients, which lets the virus spread. No approved vaccine exists for the Bundibugyo species; trials began in October.

stories.everyday: Corruption cases like this explain why citizens in many countries, including Poland, care about independent prosecutors and courts.
stories.rankWhy: Hungary's new government is prosecuting alleged corruption from the Orbán era, a test of the rule of law.
stories.title: Hungarian investigators find about $19.5 million in cash, some buried in forests, in a corruption probe into an Orbán-era minister
stories.what: Hungary's new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said searches on 12–13 November in Budapest and three other areas found cash in forints, euros and dollars hidden in farm buildings, warehouses, a home, a safe and buried in forests (Al Jazeera). Al Jazeera's report gives $19.5 million; Polish TVN24 reported about €18 million. The main suspect, Miklós Seszták, development minister in 2014–2018, is suspected of taking more than $37.2 million in bribes and kickbacks linked to overpriced second-hand buses and state construction; he was detained in September and denies wrongdoing. Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party ended Viktor Orbán's 16 years in power in April, called the find the end of the 'Fidesz-KDNP mafia'; Orbán accuses the government of using the probes to push him out of politics.
stories.why: Kickbacks raise the price the state pays for goods and services, so taxpayers lose money and public services get worse. Hungarian voters care too: a Median poll for HVG found 70% consider investigating suspected Orbán-era corruption very important (Al Jazeera).

stories.everyday: Little direct effect on daily life in Europe, but it shows how wars in Africa shape global institutions.
stories.rankWhy: Congo, the largest French-speaking country by population, threatens to quit the 90-member Francophonie over a Rwanda-linked leadership race, reflecting the war in eastern Congo.
stories.title: Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia overshadowed by a Congo–Rwanda clash before Monday's vote for secretary-general
stories.what: Leaders of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), a grouping of 90 states and governments that use French, opened a summit in Phnom Penh on Sunday, with France's Emmanuel Macron and Canada's Mark Carney attending (Al Jazeera, AFP via The Star). Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, secretary-general since 2018, is seeking a third term in Monday's vote; DR Congo has threatened to leave if she is re-elected, accusing Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group, which Rwanda denies. Congo said it was withdrawing its candidate Juliana Lumumba to back Romania's former prime minister Dacian Cioloș as a unifying candidate; Mauritania's Coumba Ba is also running. Rwanda says Macron asked Kagame to withdraw Mushikiwabo's candidacy, which Kigali refused.
stories.why: Leadership of international organisations is a tool of influence, so the conflict in eastern Congo spills into diplomacy. The OIF already lost Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso after their military governments left; losing Congo would be a bigger blow.

stories.everyday: Unclear court status can delay rulings that affect citizens and businesses, and it is one of the issues behind Poland's long-running rule-of-law debate with the EU.
stories.rankWhy: The dispute over Poland's Constitutional Tribunal affects which court rulings are recognised and how laws are reviewed.
stories.title: Poland's parties clash over a 'constitutional reset' before Monday's presidential talks on the Constitutional Tribunal, which KO and the Left will not attend
stories.what: President Karol Nawrocki has invited parliamentary groups to consultations on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) at the Belweder Palace on Monday 16 November, led by the head of his chancellery, Zbigniew Bogucki (TVN24, RMF24). Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday he would not attend, Nowa Lewica rejected the invitation and KO also refused talks. On TVN24's Sunday programme, KO's Bartosz Arłukowicz rejected a 'reset', Konfederacja's Anna Bryłka said one needs two-thirds of the Sejm, and presidential minister Błażej Poboży said the president acts as an arbiter. The dispute escalated in late October when judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska suspended TK president Bogdan Święczkowski; the president and the right-wing opposition do not recognise the tribunal's subsequent actions.
stories.why: A constitutional court checks whether laws comply with the constitution; if politicians disagree about who its legitimate judges are, its rulings are disputed and legal certainty suffers. Changing the rules permanently would require a constitutional amendment, which needs a two-thirds majority in the Sejm that no camp has.

stories.everyday: Decisions on fossil fuels and electrification influence the EU's climate rules, which shape energy and heating costs in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The talks decide how the world follows up on fossil fuels and finance for climate adaptation, which affects energy policy and vulnerable countries everywhere.
stories.title: COP31 climate talks enter their final week on Monday, with ministers taking over and a first draft of the main decision expected
stories.what: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, which opened on 9 November, begins its second and final week on 16 November, when ministers take over the hardest issues (Hürriyet Daily News; Climate Home News). Climate Home reported that a first draft of the 'cover decision', the main political statement agreed by consensus, is expected early this week. Disputes include African countries' demand to triple adaptation finance to at least $120 billion a year by 2035, how to refer to a voluntary roadmap away from coal, oil and gas launched by Brazil, and a pledge to raise electricity's share of energy use to 35% by 2035 (sources differ on today's share: about 20% per Türkiye's presidency, 23% per Climate Home). Thousands marched in Antalya on Saturday for climate finance and an end to fossil fuels.
stories.why: Adaptation finance pays for defences against climate damage, such as flood walls and drought-resistant farming; poorer countries say they cannot afford them alone. Because COP decisions need consensus, any large group can block wording it dislikes, so final texts are often compromises.

stories.everyday: Little direct effect in Europe; it shows how oil money can fund armed groups.
stories.rankWhy: Iraq is a major oil exporter; a crackdown on smuggling by an Iran-backed armed group tests the state's control over its own oil.
stories.title: Iraq's prime minister sacks nine officials over alleged oil smuggling in a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
stories.what: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander and the head of the Oil Ministry's pipelines company, after a committee confirmed intelligence about oil smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr (also called Jurf al-Sakher), military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said (Al Jazeera; The New Arab, AFP). Those accused were referred to the courts. Al Jazeera's correspondent said the network was worth up to $30 million a month, citing reports that two pipelines south of Baghdad had been tapped. Kataib Hezbollah, designated a terrorist group by Washington, has accused al-Zaidi of corruption.
stories.why: Smuggled oil gives armed groups their own income outside state control; cutting it weakens them, which is why an Atlantic Council analyst quoted by Al Jazeera described the move as tied to disarming militias. It also matters for US sanctions, since Washington has accused Iraqi groups of blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

stories.everyday: No direct effect in Poland; it is an early sign of how Gulf investors read the weekend's news.
stories.rankWhy: Saudi Arabia's market trades on Sundays, so it is the first big exchange to react to weekend news from the Gulf war.
stories.title: Saudi stocks slip 0.57% in Sunday trading as investors stay cautious
stories.what: The Tadawul All Share Index (TASI) fell 0.57% to 10,267.64 on Sunday, Business Upturn reported, describing modest selling and mild risk aversion with mixed sector performance. The Saudi exchange trades Sunday to Thursday, unlike most world markets.
stories.why: The report cited no single cause. Weekend attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia and Iran's strikes on Bahrain are the backdrop, but no source in this run linked Sunday's fall directly to them.

stories.everyday: Remittances (money sent home by emigrants) matter a lot to small economies like Cape Verde, as they once did for many Polish families.
stories.rankWhy: A peaceful election in one of Africa's most stable democracies, with its first woman presidential candidate.
stories.title: Cape Verde votes for president; incumbent José Maria Neves faces the country's first woman candidate, Joana Rosa
stories.what: Polls opened on Sunday for more than 300,000 eligible voters, including nearly 77,000 registered abroad (Al Jazeera). President José Maria Neves, 66, of the PAICV seeks a second term; his main challenger is former justice minister Joana Rosa of the Movement for Democracy (MpD), the first woman to run since independence in 1975, and six candidates are standing in total. A candidate needs more than 50%, otherwise a run-off is held on 29 November; Euronews said provisional results were expected overnight, Al Jazeera within two to three days.
stories.why: Emigration driven by a lack of jobs is the central issue: more Cape Verdeans live abroad than the roughly 500,000 on the islands (Al Jazeera). The president has a veto and a mediating role in a mixed parliamentary–presidential system.

stories.everyday: Similar debates about conscription, housing and living costs are under way across Europe, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Youth protests over education, living costs and conscription are spreading in Germany, with a Europe-wide youth strike planned for 20 November.
stories.title: At least 20 arrested at a 'Gen Z' march in Berlin; organisers plan a Europe-wide youth strike on 20 November
stories.what: Berlin police said on Sunday at least 20 people were arrested at Saturday's 'Gen Z regelt' march, with 700 officers deployed, 28 criminal complaints filed and at least three officers injured (Anadolu via Express Tribune). The movement's daytime protests in more than 30 German cities have drawn tens of thousands of young people demanding more education funding, relief from living costs and opposing plans to revive compulsory military service. A Europe-wide youth strike is planned for 20 November, with 15,000 people registered for Berlin.
stories.why: Young people face high housing costs and fear being drafted as Germany expands its army in response to Russia, so economic and security policy meet on the street.

stories.everyday: When independent reporting shrinks, people inside and outside the country get less reliable information about the conflict.
stories.rankWhy: Arrest warrants against exiled journalists and critics narrow press freedom in the Sahel.
stories.title: Burkina Faso's military government issues arrest warrants for about 20 people, including exiled journalists, on terrorism-related charges
stories.what: Burkina Faso issued 14 warrants with extradition requests and seven standard warrants on Friday, targeting exiled journalists, activists, a former minister and former officers, according to the attorney general of the Ouagadougou Court of Appeal (Africanews, AFP). Those named include RFI journalist Newton Ahmed Barry and former foreign minister Djibril Bassolé. Charges include complicity in terrorism, 'glorification of terrorism' and undermining army morale; prosecutors also asked Meta to help identify administrators of pages they say glorify terrorism.
stories.why: Africanews (AFP) reported that the military leadership that seized power in September 2022 has cracked down hard on criticism. When charges such as 'glorification of terrorism' are applied to commentary, journalists abroad as well as at home face legal risk.

stories.everyday: Domestic violence is a concern in every European country, including Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A small but unusual protest that highlights violence against women as a men's issue.
stories.title: Hundreds of men march in Bern against violence against women
stories.what: Hundreds of men rallied outside the Swiss parliament in Bern on Saturday at a 'Men Against Violence Against Women' event co-organised by social worker Christoph Gosteli and the group maenner (Al Jazeera). Justice Minister Beat Jans said in a 2 November speech that men commit four-fifths of violent crimes. A June study by the University of Zurich and MenCare found half of male respondents aged 18–24 held a dominance-based view of masculinity.
stories.why: Organisers argue that men must challenge violence among other men, rather than leaving the issue to women's groups.

stories.everyday: No direct effect yet.
stories.rankWhy: An early sign of positioning for the 2028 US presidential race after the midterms.
stories.title: New York City's Democratic Socialists urge Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028
stories.what: Delegates of the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America voted 291 to 123 on Saturday for a resolution urging Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028 (Al Jazeera). It is not a national DSA endorsement. Ocasio-Cortez has said she will decide on her future after the midterm elections.
stories.why: Activist groups try to shape a party's field early, before primaries begin.

stories.everyday: Of interest mainly to Catholics.
stories.rankWhy: A religious event of great importance to Peru's Catholics, with limited effect elsewhere.
stories.title: Pope Leo XIV leads prayers in Cusco high in the Andes as his Peru visit nears its end
stories.what: Pope Leo XIV, who once led the diocese of Chiclayo in Peru, prayed the Angelus in Cusco on Sunday and met the faithful at the Saqsaywaman archaeological park (Vatican). In his address he rejected the idea that illness reduces a person's worth and entrusted the sick to Mary.
stories.why: Papal visits draw huge crowds and focus attention on local problems; earlier in the trip he spoke about violence in Peru.

Developing: Iranian claims of mine strikes and drone attacks in the Gulf; Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia; recovery of US flight schedules.
